newsitem.title: GREECE: CASH ROW HALTS WORK IN FOUR ATHENS METRO SITES.
newsitem.headline: CASH ROW HALTS WORK IN FOUR ATHENS METRO SITES.

text.p: A cash row has stopped construction on some parts of the new Athens metro, one of Europe's biggest public works projects, officials said on Tuesday.
The two giant tunnel boring machines have been halted and work in four of 50 worksites stopped in the row between the managing company, Attiko Metro, and the contractor, Olympic Metro.

"We have a meeting at the Environment Ministry with the contractor on Thursday but I don't believe we will find common ground. It will take a number of meetings to sort things out," a senior Attiko Metro official told Reuters.

Olympic Metro is a consortium of 23 Greek and foreign firms -- including Germany's Hochtief and Siemens -- building the 520 billion drachma project. It wants 130 billion more to continue work but Attiko Metro describes the sum as unacceptable.

"They wrote us a letter this summer citing various problems which we think can be solved for a maximum 25 billion extra. But in any case they had no right to stop the work," the official, who requested anonymity, said.
The contractor has laid off 150 of 3,400 workers involved in the project to put pressure on Attiko Metro and halted works in the Omonia, Daphni, Deligianni and Attiki stations.
"We have warned them that if they continue on this path, we will find another contractor. We have the right to do it," the official said.
The project is now 50 percent complete and the opening ceremony is scheduled in the first three months of 1999.
Up to 90 percent of the project is funded with loans and subsidies from the European Union and the European Investment Bank, with Greece forking out the remaining 10 percent.
The subway will crisscross the capital with two new lines. It has been delayed already by 18 months due to archaeological finds which cost Attiko Metro about 70 billion drachmas to work around.

Work on the Metro has caused chaos in Athens, already notorious for its traffic jams, but has also underlined the urgent need for a metro system in one of the world's most polluted cities, with 1.5 million cars packing its narrow streets each day.

City planners estimate the subway will reduce the number of cars in the centre by some 250,000 and reduce car exhaust pollution by 35 percent, a boon in a city forever covered by a layer of grey smog. --Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
